set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: Under the modified Duke criteria, in which situation is transesophageal echocardiography required for optimal assessment?
opts: A stable murmur known for years
An unchanged long-standing murmur does not meet the endocardial involvement criterion; the transesophageal study is required for possible prosthetic valve or complicated endocarditis.
Prophylaxis is decided by the cardiac condition and the procedure, not by imaging; the transesophageal study is for possible prosthetic valve endocarditis.
Fever alone is one minor criterion and does not call for this study; transesophageal echocardiography is required for possible prosthetic valve or complicated disease.
Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is required for optimal assessment of possible prosthetic valve endocarditis or complicated endocarditis; it is highly sensitive and specific.

set1.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set1.q: Under the modified Duke criteria, Osler nodes count as which minor criterion?
opts: Correct. Osler nodes are an immunologic phenomenon, the minor criterion that also holds glomerulonephritis, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor.
Vascular phenomena are emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages and Janeway lesions; Osler nodes are immunologic.
Microbiologic evidence is a positive culture that misses the major criterion. Osler nodes are an immunologic phenomenon.
Predisposition means a predisposing heart condition or injection drug use. Osler nodes are an immunologic phenomenon.

set1.q: Which organism causes the most lethal infective endocarditis?
opts: The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms are not named as the most lethal; Staphylococcus aureus is.
Enterococci are hard to treat because of resistance, but Staphylococcus aureus is named the most lethal organism.
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most lethal organism, with mortality highest in prosthetic valve endocarditis and lower in people who inject drugs.
Viridans streptococcal endocarditis has a relatively good prognosis if antibiotics start before complications occur.

set1.q: Which consultant manages antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring in infective endocarditis?
opts: Addiction medicine provides harm reduction for people who inject drugs, not the antibiotic plan.
Palliative care is part of multidisciplinary disposition planning; antibiotics and monitoring belong to infectious disease.
Correct. Infectious disease is consulted for antibiotic therapy and outpatient monitoring pending disposition; cardiothoracic surgery evaluates surgery and anticoagulation needs.
Cardiothoracic surgery evaluates the need for surgery and anticoagulation, not the antibiotic plan.

set1.q: Janeway lesions are particularly associated with which form of infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Janeway lesions, painless hemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles from septic emboli, are associated with acute infective endocarditis.
Janeway lesions come from septic emboli, which fit the acute form that seeds extracardiac sites; subacute disease rarely metastasizes.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis in lupus is non-infective and does not produce septic emboli. Janeway lesions are associated with acute infective endocarditis.
Janeway lesions mark active septic emboli, not healed disease. They are associated with acute infective endocarditis.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Roughly what share of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated?
opts: The health care-associated share is not trivial. About a quarter to a third of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated.
Correct. About 25-35% of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated, which is why recent hospitalization and lines matter in the history.
Half overstates it. About 25-35% of native valve endocarditis is health care-associated, the rest community-acquired.
Most native valve endocarditis is still community-acquired. The health care-associated share is about 25-35%.

set1.q: Which autoimmune disease can produce a non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis that mimics infective endocarditis?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis is not the disease named with Libman-Sacks endocarditis; systemic lupus erythematosus is.
Correct. Systemic lupus erythematosus may present with non-infective (Libman-Sacks) endocarditis, so it sits in the autoimmune differential of infective endocarditis.
Polymyalgia rheumatica mimics endocarditis with myalgia and elevated inflammatory markers, not with a valve lesion of its own.
Reactive arthritis is in the differential for its joint symptoms, but the non-infective Libman-Sacks lesion belongs to lupus.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: Which prophylaxis fits a penicillin-allergic patient who cannot take oral medication?
opts: Ampicillin is a penicillin; it is the injectable choice only for patients without a penicillin allergy.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cephalexin is an oral option, and this patient cannot take oral medication; cefazolin or ceftriaxone is given by injection.
ruled out by a stated finding
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

Correct. Penicillin-allergic patients unable to take oral medication receive cefazolin or ceftriaxone intramuscularly or intravenously, provided there is no history of anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin.

set1.q: Why does a new murmur develop in infective endocarditis?
opts: Narrowing of a coronary artery by plaque
Coronary narrowing does not cause a murmur. Valvular damage or rupture of the chordae tendineae does.
Valve damage or chordae tendineae rupture
Correct. A new cardiac murmur is due to valvular damage or rupture of the chordae tendineae, which leads to regurgitation.
Increased flow from a high-output fever
Fever can produce a flow murmur, but the new murmur of endocarditis comes from valve damage or chordae rupture.
A friction rub is pericardial, not a murmur. The new murmur reflects valve damage or chordal rupture.

set1.q: When should empiric antibiotics be started for suspected infective endocarditis?
opts: Before any cultures, to save time
Giving antibiotics before cultures can sterilize them and lose the organism. Cultures come first, then empiric therapy.
The echocardiogram is not the gate. Empiric antibiotics follow the blood cultures.
Only once the organism is known
Waiting for the final organism delays treatment. Empiric therapy starts after cultures are drawn and is tailored later.
Only after blood cultures are drawn
Correct. Empiric therapy is started only after blood cultures have been drawn, because antibiotics given first can leave the cultures negative.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Which kind of antibiotic therapy does infective endocarditis require?
opts: Lifelong suppression is not the standard. Therapy is bactericidal, parenteral and prolonged for weeks, then stopped.
Correct. All bacteria in the vegetation must be killed, so therapy must be bactericidal and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture, and given parenterally.
Bacteriostatic drugs only halt growth, and a brief course cannot sterilize a vegetation. Therapy is bactericidal and prolonged.
Three days is far too short. Endocarditis needs bactericidal therapy for typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set1.q: In a child with endocarditis, a fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers suggests which organisms?
opts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are tied to prosthetic material and neonatal lines, not fulminant spiking fevers in children.
Fungal disease is linked to neonatal central lines. Fulminant high fevers suggest pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.
Correct. Children usually have an indolent course, but a fulminant presentation with high spiking fevers suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus.
Viridans streptococci cause the usual indolent pediatric course; a fulminant picture suggests pneumococcus or Staphylococcus aureus.

set1.q: How are the petechiae of infective endocarditis described?
opts: Large bruises that spread over days
Petechiae are minute hemorrhages, not large spreading bruises, and they can be transient.
Firm nodules that last for months
Petechiae are flat, minute hemorrhages, not firm nodules, and they can be transient rather than lasting for months.
Correct. The petechiae of infective endocarditis are minute hemorrhages, and they can be transient, fading rather than persisting.
Painful nodules on the finger pads
Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads are Osler nodes. Petechiae are minute hemorrhages that can be transient.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Which organism causes fungal infective endocarditis?
opts: Kingella is a gram-negative HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) bacterium, not a fungus.
Eikenella corrodens is a gram-negative HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) bacterium. The fungal cause named is Candida.
Enterococcus is a gram-positive bacterium from the genitourinary tract. The fungal cause of endocarditis is Candida.
Correct. Fungal infective endocarditis is caused by Candida (and Aspergillus); fungal infection is difficult to cure with medication alone and is an indication for surgery.

set1.q: When is the risk of prosthetic valve endocarditis greatest?
opts: Ten or more years after replacement
Risk does not climb with time. It is highest in the first year and gradually declines toward native-valve risk afterward.
The operation is not the only window. Risk stays highest across the whole first year after replacement, then declines.
Equal at every point after surgery
Risk is not flat. It peaks in the first year after the replacement and then declines until it resembles native-valve risk.
Within the first year after replacement
Correct. The greatest risk is within the first year after valve replacement; it then gradually declines until it is similar to the risk for a native valve.

set1.q: Which antibiotic treats infective endocarditis caused by the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group?
opts: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin; the gram-negative HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms are treated with ceftriaxone.
Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, not the gram-negative HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group.
Rifampin is an add-on for staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection, not HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) therapy, which is ceftriaxone.
Correct. HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam.

set1.q: What is the role of anticoagulation in native valve infective endocarditis?
opts: Vegetations are treated by killing the bacteria with antibiotics. Anticoagulation is not beneficial in native valve infection.
Correct. Anticoagulation is not beneficial in patients with native valve infection, and it is controversial in patients with prosthetic valves.
Anticoagulation does not prevent septic emboli and is not beneficial in native valve endocarditis.
Routine anticoagulation is not required; it is not beneficial for native valves and controversial for prosthetic ones.

set1.q: Which sex is affected more often by infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Men are affected more often than women, one of the epidemiologic features listed with older age, injection drug use and poor dentition.
Women are not the majority. Men are affected more often than women among patients with infective endocarditis.
The sexes are not affected equally; men outnumber women among patients with infective endocarditis.
Postmenopausal women are not singled out. Men are affected more often than women among patients with infective endocarditis.

set1.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set1.q: In a high-risk patient, what is recommended about prophylaxis for transesophageal echocardiography, upper endoscopy, colonoscopy or cystoscopy?
opts: It is not needed without infection
Correct. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for nondental procedures such as transesophageal echocardiography, upper endoscopy, colonoscopy or cystoscopy in the absence of active infection.
It is required before each one
These nondental procedures do not call for prophylaxis even in high-risk patients, absent active infection.
It is needed for colonoscopy and cystoscopy
Colonoscopy and cystoscopy are on the same no-prophylaxis list as upper endoscopy and transesophageal echocardiography, absent active infection.
It is given as a 7-day course
Prophylaxis is never a week-long course, and for these procedures it is not recommended at all without infection.

set1.q: What is a perivalvular abscess?
opts: Infection extending past the leaflets into the myocardium
Correct. A perivalvular abscess forms when infection extends beyond the valve leaflets into the myocardial tissue around the valve.
A sterile clot sitting on a prosthetic valve sewing ring
A sterile clot is a thrombus, not an abscess. A perivalvular abscess is infection extending beyond the leaflets into the myocardium.
Pus collecting in the pericardial sac after surgery
Pus in the pericardial sac is purulent pericarditis. A perivalvular abscess sits in the myocardium around the valve.
A pocket infection around a pacemaker generator
A generator pocket infection is a device infection under the skin. A perivalvular abscess extends from the valve into the myocardium.

set1.q: Which urinalysis findings are expected in infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Urinalysis can show hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria, reflecting renal involvement such as glomerulonephritis or emboli.
Glucose and ketones in urine point to diabetes, not to endocarditis, whose urinalysis shows hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.
Urine bilirubin suggests liver disease. Endocarditis brings hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria.
The urine is often abnormal: hematuria, proteinuria and pyuria are listed findings.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: How is bacteremia defined?
opts: Inflammation of the inner lining of the heart
Inflammation of the inner lining of the heart is endocarditis. Bacteremia is bacteria in the bloodstream, identified by a true-positive blood culture.
A vegetation seen on transesophageal imaging
A vegetation on transesophageal echocardiogram is evidence of endocardial involvement, a separate major Duke criterion. Bacteremia is defined by a true-positive blood culture.
A fever above 38 degrees Celsius with chills
Fever with chills is a symptom and only a minor Duke criterion. Bacteremia is the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream, shown by a true-positive blood culture.
Bacteria detected on a true-positive blood culture
Correct. Bacteremia is the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream, identified by detection of any true-positive blood culture. Blood should normally be sterile.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: How long do Osler nodes typically last?
opts: They last minutes, like an urticarial wheal
Osler nodes are not that fleeting. They appear in crops and fade over 2-3 days, and they are painful.
They grow steadily until antibiotics stop
Osler nodes do not grow steadily while untreated; they come in crops and fade in 2-3 days.
They appear in crops and fade in 2 to 3 days
Correct. Osler nodes appear in crops and fade in 2-3 days; they are painful and reflect an immunologic phenomenon.
They persist for months and scar the skin
Osler nodes are transient, not permanent. They appear in crops and fade within 2-3 days.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: Which prophylaxis fits a patient with no penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication?
opts: Doxycycline is an oral option for penicillin-allergic patients; this patient cannot take oral medication and is not allergic.
ruled out by a stated finding
Vancomycin is not part of the standard prophylaxis table for adults. Ampicillin intramuscular or intravenous is.
Correct. A patient without penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication gets ampicillin intramuscularly or intravenously 30-60 minutes before the procedure (or cefazolin or ceftriaxone).
Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.

set1.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set1.q: Which cardiac condition warrants endocarditis prophylaxis before dental work?
opts: Hypertension is not a high-risk condition for prophylaxis. Previous infective endocarditis is.
Coronary bypass grafting is not on the high-risk list; previous infective endocarditis is.
Correct. Previous infective endocarditis is a high-risk condition, with prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, certain congenital heart disease, and cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation.
Coronary stents are not on the high-risk list. Previous infective endocarditis is.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Infective endocarditis is classified by temporal evolution, by site, by predisposing risk factor and by which other feature?
opts: Murmur grade is an exam finding, not a classification axis. The cause of infection, such as the organism, completes the four.
The cause, such as the organism

Correct. Classification uses temporal evolution (acute or subacute), site (native, prosthetic or device), cause of infection (methicillin-resistant or -susceptible Staphylococcus aureus) and predisposing risk factors such as injection drug use.
Vegetation size is not one of the four axes. The axes are timing, site, cause of infection and predisposing risk factors.
Stenosis severity is not a classification axis. Infective endocarditis is classified by timing, site, cause (organism) and predisposing risk factors.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: A gastrointestinal source of bacteremia points to which endocarditis organism?
opts: Viridans streptococci come from the oral cavity, not the gastrointestinal tract, whose organism is Streptococcus gallolyticus.
Kingella is a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism from the upper respiratory tract. The gastrointestinal organism is Streptococcus gallolyticus.
Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative skin organism tied to early prosthetic valve infection, not to a gastrointestinal source.
Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus is the gastrointestinal-tract organism among the causes of infective endocarditis.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Which antibiotic is preferred for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of a native valve?
opts: Ampicillin plus gentamicin is an enterococcal regimen. Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus gets nafcillin or oxacillin.

Correct. Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is treated with nafcillin or oxacillin, or cefazolin; vancomycin is the drug for methicillin-resistant strains and only an alternative for susceptible ones.

Vancomycin or daptomycin is the regimen for methicillin-resistant strains; for susceptible strains vancomycin is only an alternative when a beta-lactam cannot be used, so nafcillin or oxacillin is preferred.
Ceftriaxone is the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) and streptococcal option. Susceptible staphylococci get nafcillin or oxacillin, or cefazolin.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Which organisms cause the largest share of endocarditis on implantable electronic devices?
opts: Correct. Coagulase-negative staphylococci cause about 41% of device endocarditis, with Staphylococcus aureus close behind at about 36%.
Streptococci cause only about 2% of device endocarditis. Skin staphylococci, led by the coagulase-negative species, dominate.

The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract and are not a leading device organism; coagulase-negative staphylococci lead at about 41%.
Enterococci cause about 4% of device endocarditis. Coagulase-negative staphylococci cause about 41%.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set1.q: Subacute infective endocarditis is gradually progressive unless what happens?
opts: Fever level does not define the turning point. A major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic aneurysm does.
A softer murmur is not the listed complication. Subacute disease turns abrupt with a major embolus or a ruptured mycotic aneurysm.
A major embolus or aneurysm rupture
Correct. Subacute endocarditis is gradually progressive unless complicated by a major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic (infected) aneurysm.
The patient starts a daily aspirin
Aspirin does not change the course described. A major embolic event or a ruptured mycotic aneurysm is what interrupts the slow progression.

set2.q: In people who inject drugs, what share of tricuspid valve endocarditis is caused by Staphylococcus aureus?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus dominates, not the reverse: 80-90% of tricuspid valve infections in people who inject drugs.
Staphylococcus aureus is not a minor player here. It causes 80-90% of tricuspid valve infections in people who inject drugs.
30-40% is far too low. In people who inject drugs with tricuspid involvement, Staphylococcus aureus causes 80-90%.
Correct. In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus causes more than 60% of all endocarditis and 80-90% of cases where the tricuspid valve is infected.

set2.q: Which disorder in the differential of infective endocarditis causes myalgia with elevated inflammatory markers?
opts: Correct. Polymyalgia rheumatica presents with myalgia and elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein), mimicking the constitutional picture of endocarditis.
Antiphospholipid syndrome mimics endocarditis through thromboemboli and cardiac valve disease, not through myalgia.
Atrial myxoma mimics endocarditis with fever and a new murmur, not with myalgia and inflammatory markers.
Tuberculosis mimics endocarditis with fever, night sweats and weight loss. Myalgia with high inflammatory markers is polymyalgia rheumatica.

set2.q: What is the most likely complication of fungal infective endocarditis?
opts: Conduction block follows abscess extension into the septum. Fungal endocarditis most likely embolizes to large peripheral arteries.
Fungal endocarditis does not resolve on its own; it is hard to cure even with medication and is an indication for surgery.
Painful nodules on the finger pads
Osler nodes are an immunologic sign, not the leading fungal complication, which is embolic occlusion of large peripheral arteries.
Correct. In fungal endocarditis the most likely complication is embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries from embolization.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: In a high-risk patient, which oral event does not call for endocarditis prophylaxis?
opts: Correct. Bleeding from trauma to the lips or oral mucosa is on the list that does not require prophylaxis, with dental radiographs and orthodontic adjustments.
Scaling manipulates the gingival tissue, so it calls for prophylaxis in a high-risk patient.
Extraction manipulates the gums and root, so it calls for prophylaxis in a high-risk patient.
Biopsy perforates the oral mucosa, so it calls for prophylaxis in a high-risk patient.

set2.q: A perivalvular abscess that extends into the upper ventricular septum causes which complication?
opts: A mycotic (infected) aneurysm is an arterial complication. Septal extension of an abscess interrupts the conduction system.
The lung is a listed embolic site, but emboli do not interrupt conduction; an abscess extending into the upper ventricular septum does.
Correct. When the abscess extends into the upper ventricular septum it can interrupt the conduction system; extension into the epicardium causes pericarditis.
Pericarditis follows extension into the epicardium. Extension into the upper ventricular septum interrupts the conduction system.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group of endocarditis organisms comes from which source?
opts: Correct. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract.
The genitourinary tract is the source of enterococci, not the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms, which come from the upper respiratory tract.
The skin is the source of staphylococci. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms come from the upper respiratory tract.
The gastrointestinal tract is the source of Streptococcus gallolyticus. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group comes from the upper respiratory tract.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for infective endocarditis for the following populations. 8. infant 9. child 10. adolescent 11. adult 12. elderly
set2.q: In infants, which complications are common because septic emboli are frequent?
opts: Heart failure is less common in pediatric disease. Septic emboli cause osteomyelitis, meningitis and pneumonia.
Peripheral stigmata are less common in children. Infants' septic emboli cause osteomyelitis, meningitis and pneumonia.
Correct. Septic emboli are common in neonates and infants, producing osteomyelitis, meningitis or pneumonia, and neurologic signs such as seizures, hemiparesis and apnea are frequent.
Immunologic phenomena are not the listed infant complications. Septic emboli cause osteomyelitis, meningitis and pneumonia.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which is the most common indication for surgery in infective endocarditis?
opts: Fever on the third hospital day
Early persistent fever alone is not the indication. Heart failure from valvular dysfunction leads the list.
Correct. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery; others are failure to resolve on appropriate antibiotics, abscess and fungal infection.
A vegetation alone is not the leading indication. Heart failure from valvular dysfunction is.
A positive culture starts antibiotics, not surgery. Heart failure from valve dysfunction is the most common surgical indication.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Why is fungal infective endocarditis an indication for surgery?
opts: It is hard to cure with medication alone
Correct. Fungal infection is difficult to cure with medications alone, so it joins heart failure, persistent infection and abscess as an indication for surgery.
Pericarditis follows abscess extension into the epicardium, not fungal infection as such. Fungal infection is hard to cure medically.
Intravenous antifungals exist. The reason is that fungal endocarditis is difficult to cure with medication alone.
Fungi do not grow in blood cultures
Cultures can grow Candida. Surgery is indicated because fungal infection is hard to cure with drugs alone.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which description fits Janeway lesions?
opts: White-centered hemorrhages seen in the retina
White-centered retinal hemorrhages are Roth spots. Janeway lesions are painless macules on the palms and soles.
Thin dark lines under the proximal nail plate
Dark lines under the nails are splinter hemorrhages. Janeway lesions are painless hemorrhagic macules on palms and soles.
Painless hemorrhagic macules on palms and soles
Correct. Janeway lesions are nontender hemorrhagic lesions on the soles of the feet and palms of the hands, from septic emboli, and are associated with acute infective endocarditis.
Painful nodules on the pads of fingers and toes
Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads are Osler nodes, an immunologic phenomenon, not Janeway lesions.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: When the presentation suggests acute endocarditis, how quickly should the first cultures be drawn?
opts: No cultures until antibiotics have begun
Cultures always come before antibiotics; empiric therapy is started only after blood cultures are drawn.
Two cultures within the first 1 to 2 hours
Correct. If the presentation suggests acute bacterial endocarditis, two cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours so that empiric antibiotics are not delayed.
One culture at the end of the first day
Waiting a day is too slow for acute disease. Two cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours.
Three cultures spread over three days
Spreading cultures over days fits neither tempo. In acute disease two cultures are drawn within 1-2 hours.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: What damages non-valvular endocardium enough for infective endocarditis to take hold there?
opts: Slow flow during sleep does not injure the endocardium. Jets of blood striking the lining, or foreign bodies, are what damage it.
Lipid plaques build up in arterial walls in atherosclerosis. Damaged endocardium in infective endocarditis comes from aberrant jets or foreign bodies.
Pericardial fluid compresses the heart from outside (tamponade); it does not damage the endocardium. Aberrant jets and foreign bodies do.
Correct. Endocardium damaged by aberrant jets of blood or by foreign bodies becomes a site for infection, alongside the valves and intracardiac devices.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: In a patient at high risk, which procedure does not require endocarditis prophylaxis?
opts: Tonsillectomy incises respiratory mucosa, one of the invasive respiratory procedures that do call for prophylaxis.
Root canals manipulate the periapical region of the tooth and do call for prophylaxis in a high-risk patient.
Correct. Gastrointestinal and genitourinary procedures (cystoscopy, upper endoscopy, colonoscopy) do not require endocarditis prophylaxis.
Extractions manipulate the gums and tooth roots, so they do call for prophylaxis in a high-risk patient.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which complete blood count pattern is expected in infective endocarditis?
opts: Polycythemia is not expected. Infection raises the white count, and chronic inflammation causes a normocytic anemia.
Eosinophilia and macrocytosis are not the pattern. Leukocytosis and normocytic anemia of chronic disease are.
Correct. The complete blood count with differential shows leukocytosis and anemia of chronic disease with a normal mean corpuscular volume (normocytic).
A low white count with small red cells is not the expected pattern. Expect leukocytosis and normocytic anemia of chronic disease.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Where are splinter hemorrhages found?
opts: In the retina, with a white center
White-centered retinal hemorrhages are Roth spots. Splinter hemorrhages lie under the nails.
On the hard palate and conjunctiva
The palate and conjunctiva are where petechiae appear. Splinter hemorrhages lie under the fingernails and toenails.
On the pads of the fingers and toes
Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads are Osler nodes. Splinter hemorrhages are lines under the nails.
Correct. Splinter hemorrhages are found under the fingernails and toenails, in the proximal portion of the nail plate, as an embolic phenomenon.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which course is typical of subacute infective endocarditis?
opts: Low fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks
Correct. Subacute infective endocarditis has an indolent course: lower fevers, generalized malaise and weight loss over weeks or months, with slow structural damage, if any.
High fevers and toxicity within a few days
High fevers and systemic toxicity over 3-10 days describe acute infective endocarditis, caused by a virulent, invasive organism.
Sudden collapse with no preceding illness
Sudden collapse is not the subacute picture. Subacute disease smolders with low fevers, malaise and weight loss.
Painful joints that migrate every few hours
Migratory arthritis is not the pattern described. Subacute endocarditis smolders with low fevers, malaise and weight loss over weeks or months.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: On which side of a ventricular septal defect does infective endocarditis develop?
opts: The high-pressure (left) side drives the jet but is not where the lesion lands. Endocarditis develops on the low-pressure (right) side of the defect.
The defect is not involved symmetrically. Infection settles on the low-pressure side, where the aberrant jet damages the endocardium.
Valves are the most common site, but not the only one: the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect is also a recognized site.
Correct. Infective endocarditis can affect the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect, where the jet of blood strikes and damages the endocardium; the right side is the low-pressure side.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which organism causes the largest share of health care-associated native valve endocarditis?
opts: Streptococci as a group lead community-acquired native valve endocarditis (about 40%) but cause only about 13% of health care-associated cases.
Enterococci cause about 16% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis; Staphylococcus aureus causes about 52%.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci cause about 11% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis; Staphylococcus aureus causes about 52%.
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus causes about 52% of health care-associated native valve endocarditis, against about 28% of community-acquired cases.

set2.io: Discuss indications and antibiotic regimens for subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis.
set2.q: Why is clindamycin no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis?
opts: Correct. Clindamycin is no longer recommended for prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection.
QT prolongation is not the stated reason. Clindamycin was dropped because of Clostridioides difficile risk.
Coverage was not the stated problem; the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection is.
It must be given for weeks
Prophylaxis is a single dose whatever the drug. Clindamycin was dropped for its Clostridioides difficile risk.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: In Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis, mortality is highest in which group?
opts: Native valve disease in people who do not inject drugs carries about 30% mortality, lower than prosthetic valve infection.
Pediatric mortality is 5-16% overall. The highest Staphylococcus aureus mortality is in prosthetic valve endocarditis.
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus mortality is about 50% in prosthetic valve endocarditis, higher than in non-injecting patients (about 30%) and people who inject drugs (about 5%).
People who inject drugs have the lowest stated Staphylococcus aureus mortality, about 5%.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which organism belongs to the fastidious gram-negative group of endocarditis organisms from the upper respiratory tract?
opts: Streptococcus gallolyticus is the gastrointestinal-source streptococcus, not one of the gram-negative HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organisms.

Correct. The HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group is Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens and Kingella species, from the upper respiratory tract.
Enterococcus faecalis is an enterococcus from the genitourinary tract, not a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism.

Staphylococcus lugdunensis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that sometimes causes acute endocarditis; it is not a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism.

set2.q: For how long after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is prophylaxis warranted?
opts: Six weeks is too short. The high-risk window after repair with prosthetic material is the first 6 months.
Correct. The first 6 months after congenital heart disease repair with prosthetic material or a device is a high-risk period that warrants prophylaxis.
Five years is too long for a repair without residual defects; the window is the first 6 months.
Lifelong prophylaxis applies to conditions such as prior endocarditis or residual defects, not to every repair; the window here is 6 months.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Without treatment, how quickly does acute infective endocarditis progress to death?
opts: Death within hours is not the stated course. Untreated acute endocarditis progresses to death within weeks.
Correct. If untreated, acute infective endocarditis progresses to death within weeks, which is why cultures and bactericidal antibiotics cannot wait.
Several months is the indolent pace of subacute disease. Untreated acute endocarditis progresses to death within weeks.
A years-long course would be closer to subacute, indolent disease. Untreated acute endocarditis kills within weeks.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: What are Roth spots?
opts: Thin dark lines under the nails
Dark lines under the nails are splinter hemorrhages, an embolic phenomenon. Roth spots are in the retina.
Painless macules on palms and soles
Painless hemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles are Janeway lesions. Roth spots are white-centered retinal hemorrhages.
Correct. Roth spots are white-centered hemorrhages in the retina, from vasculitis affecting the small arteries of the retina.
Painful nodules on the finger pads
Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads are Osler nodes, an immunologic phenomenon, not Roth spots.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: Which single positive blood culture is excluded from the microbiologic minor criterion as a common contaminant?
opts: Streptococcus gallolyticus is a typical endocarditis organism under the major criterion, not a contaminant.
Correct. Single positive cultures for coagulase-negative staphylococci and diphtheroids are excluded because they are common culture contaminants.
Viridans streptococci are a typical endocarditis organism; two separate positive cultures meet the major criterion.
Staphylococcus aureus is a typical organism for the major criterion, not an excluded contaminant.

set2.io: Demonstrate understanding of modified Duke diagnostic criteria.
set2.q: Which combination of modified Duke criteria establishes definite infective endocarditis?
opts: Two minor criteria alone reach neither definite nor possible; possible needs three minor or one major plus one minor.
Correct. Definite endocarditis is documented by two major criteria, one major and three minor criteria, or five minor criteria.
One major plus one minor criterion makes endocarditis possible, not definite; three minor would be needed.
Three minor criteria make endocarditis possible. Definite needs five minor, one major and three minor, or two major.

Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: What causes infective endocarditis?
opts: Immune complexes alone, with no organism
Immune complexes cause some peripheral signs, such as Osler nodes, but the disease itself needs microorganisms invading and colonizing the endocardium.
Plaque rupture with thrombosis causes acute coronary syndromes. Infective endocarditis is microbial invasion and colonization of the endocardium.
Fibrous scarring of the pericardial sac
Fibrous scarring of the pericardium is constrictive pericarditis. Infective endocarditis is microbial colonization of the endocardium.
Correct. Infective endocarditis is caused by invasion and colonization of the endocardial structures by microorganisms, with resulting inflammation and a vegetation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: By which route are antibiotics for infective endocarditis given?
opts: Inhaled antibiotics treat airway infection, not a valve vegetation. Endocarditis antibiotics are parenteral.
Correct. Antibiotics should be given parenterally, with hospital admission and close monitoring of labs, renal function and cardiovascular status by a multidisciplinary team.
Oral therapy is not the standard. Endocarditis antibiotics are given parenterally, as intravenous therapy.
Topical antibiotics cannot reach a vegetation inside the heart. Therapy is parenteral.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Acute endocarditis 3. Subacute endocarditis
set2.q: Which organism is a classic cause of subacute infective endocarditis?
opts: Correct. Subacute endocarditis is caused by viridans streptococci, enterococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci and the HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) group.
Staphylococcus aureus is a virulent, invasive organism that causes acute endocarditis, with high fevers and rapid valve destruction.
Beta-hemolytic streptococci are listed with Staphylococcus aureus as causes of acute, not subacute, endocarditis.
Candida causes fungal endocarditis, a separate category. The classic bacterial cause of subacute disease is viridans streptococci.

set2.io: Discuss prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis.
set2.q: When does bronchoscopy call for endocarditis prophylaxis in a high-risk patient?
opts: Not even when a biopsy is taken
Invasive respiratory procedures that incise or biopsy the mucosa do call for prophylaxis.
Sedation is not the criterion. Incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as biopsy, is.
When the mucosa is incised, as for biopsy
Correct. Bronchoscopy needs no prophylaxis unless it involves incision of the respiratory mucosa, such as a biopsy.
Plain bronchoscopy is on the no-prophylaxis list; only incision or biopsy of the mucosa changes that.
